sources.citation: Endangered Languages Project. Jilbe [aka Zoulbou] (ELP id 4325). endangeredlanguages.com (Internet Archive copy 2023).
sources.note: Sources listed are only Dimmendaal & Voeltz 2007 (EWEL ch. 7), Ethnologue 16 (2009), UNESCO Atlas 2010 and the World Oral Literature Project; speaker figure 100 "comes from H. Tourneux"; no descriptive bibliography.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, 4th edition (draft). Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. Entry 218 Jilbe.
sources.note: "218. Jilbe 1.C Jilbe 3. Borno State, a single village on the Nigeria Cameroun border, south of Dikwa 4. ? 100 speakers (Tourneux p.c. 1999) 5. Chadic: Biu-Mandara B: Mandage group Source(s) Tourneux (1997)" — no Refs line, and 'Tourneux (1997)' has no entry in the atlas bibliography (only Tourneux & Yaya 1999 and Tourneux 2004 appear).

sources.citation: Wikipedia. Biu–Mandara languages (raw wikitext, accessed 2026-09-17), sections Gravina (2014) and Blench (2006); and Wikipedia, Jilbe language (stub).
sources.note: "Jilbe was not classified, as no sources were available." (summarising Gravina 2014); Blench 2006 lists "? Jilbe" under Mandage (Kotoko) B.1. The Jilbe stub (read via direct download, not saved) has only Ethnologue-derived facts and reports the last speaker as an elderly man in 2006.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x. Languoid jilb1238 Jilbe (Hammarström et al.). glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/jilb1238 (HTML + JSON).
sources.note: Classification Afro-Asiatic > Chadic > Biu-Mandara > Unclassified Biu-Mandara; all five references are survey entries (Glottolog's fullest description is only a wordlist); the only subclassification comment cites Gravina 2014; AES 'shifting'/threatened.

sources.citation: Blažek, Václav. 2024. Central Chadic numerals in comparative perspective. Lingua Posnaniensis 66(2): 33-71. DOI 10.14746/linpo.2024.66.2.2 (CC BY-NC-ND, open).
sources.note: Named in classification only; no data, no statement.

sources.citation: OLAC. 2021. OLAC resources in and about the Jilbe language (ISO jie). language-archives.org (Internet Archive copy).
sources.note: Catalogue lists only the Glottolog record and the Ethnologue entry; no language description, wordlist or recording exists in any OLAC archive.

sources.citation: Tourneux, Henry, Mahamat Adam & Sean Allison. 2020. Bibliographie kotoko / Kotoko Bibliography. HAL halshs-02927626.
sources.note: The specialists' general bibliography of everything written on Kotoko varieties; it is the one place that would list any Jilbe wordlist, survey note or thesis (e.g. the 'Adam 1990' cited by Rothmaler) if one exists.

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul, Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2016. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 19th ed. Dallas: SIL International. Entry "Jilbe" (jie). (Internet Archive copy of ethnologue.com/language/jie.)
sources.note: No linguistic description. "Population 100 (1999 H. Tourneux). Location Borno state: Jilbe town, Cameroon border area. 1 village. Language Status 8b (Nearly extinct). Classification Afro-Asiatic, Chadic, Biu-Mandara, B, B.1. Dialects None known. Kotoko speakers in Cameroon and Chad consistently report low intelligibility with Jilbe. Distinct from Zizilivakan [ziz]."

sources.citation: Gravina, Richard. 2014. The Phonology of Proto-Central Chadic: the reconstruction of the phonology and lexicon of Proto-Central Chadic, and the linguistic history of the Central Chadic languages. LOT Dissertation Series 375. Utrecht: LOT (Leiden PhD).
sources.note: Nothing about Jilbe: the Introduction's table of languages and data sources (p. 13, p. 41) reads verbatim "Jilbe [jie] Kotoko none" — Gravina had no Jilbe data at all; the only mention of Jilbe in the 437-page dissertation.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2012. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, 3rd edition. Entry 215 Jilbe.
sources.note: Same entry as the 4th edition (single village south of Dikwa, ? 100 speakers, Tourneux p.c. 1999, Source(s) Tourneux (1997)); no description.

sources.citation: Brenzinger, Matthias (ed.). 2007. Language Diversity Endangered. (Trends in Linguistics. Studies and Monographs 181.) Berlin / New York: Mouton de Gruyter. xvii+454 pp. [copies we hold is the complete volume; African chapters read: ch. 6 Brenzinger 'Language Endangerment in Northern Africa' 123–139; ch. 7 Blench 'Endangered Languages in West Africa' 140–162; ch. 8 Connell 'Endangered Languages in Central Africa' 163–178; ch. 9 Brenzinger 'Language Endangerment in Southern and Eastern Africa' 179–204]
sources.note: Nothing on stress/tone: table row only — 'A single village (Tourneux p.c.)'.

sources.citation: Tourneux, Henry. 1997. [title unknown — cited only as 'Tourneux (1997)' as the Source for the Jilbe entry in Blench's Atlas of Nigerian Languages, eds. III (2012) and IV (2020); no matching bibliography entry in the atlas or on HAL]
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only named data source for Jilbe anywhere; Tourneux is also the origin of the speaker count (p.c. 1999) and of any Jilbe wordlist that may exist; possibly the same work as his 1994 chapter 'Langues en voie de disparition dans le bassin du Tchad' or a Kotoko survey note.

sources.citation: Adam [Mahamat?]. 1990. [title unknown; cited as 'Adam (1990: 3)' by Rothmaler 2007, Place Names in Borno and Yobe States, for a phrase given in 'the three Kotoko dialects Jilbe, Logone, and Afade']

sources.note: Snippet: "Jilbe [62], also known as Zoulbou, is a Chadic (Afroasiatic) language, which probably has 2,000 or fewer speakers mainly living in Jilbe town.. It may be the same language as Ziziliveken. Jilbe is a genetically rather distinct member of the Kotoko (Lagwan) group.." — endangerment survey entry, no phonology.

sources.citation: Rothmaler, Eva. 2007. Place Names in Borno and Yobe States (Northern Nigeria). Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.

sources.note: Snippet: "Adam (1990: 3).. provides the translation of 'I mark this place for you to settle' in the three Kotoko dialects Jilbe, Logone, and Afade: wafiya wurta dihe, mbane waraku dihe, and ngurdu wotogu dihe" — the only trace found of primary Jilbe language data (an unaccented, untoned phrase, attributed to an 'Adam 1990' not further identified here).
